title: Tamlaght O’Crilly: the Hugh households
standfirst: Two distinct Hugh Glasgow householders appear in the 1740 return, and another Hugh appears in a 1772 parish declaration. The records do not identify either household or state kinship.
question: Which, if any, later Glasgow family belongs to each documented Hugh household?
answer: The 1740 return proves two adult Hugh Glasgow households in Tamlaght O’Crilly. It gives neither townland nor family detail, while the 1772 declaration supplies only parish membership; neither can safely be assigned to a known Hugh or used to prove descent from the traditional William. The traditional William now has a selected, very uncertain Scottish father through the Polwarth/Cavers comparison; that model does not resolve either Tamlaght identity.

chapters.period: 1639–1689 · two very uncertain fathers through possible identity
chapters.title: William Glasgow: a conditional Polwarth–Cavers–Ulster family
body: Glasgow-2462 is the proposed, very uncertain working father of the traditional Ulster ancestor Glasgow-591 and the Cavers Covenanter Glasgow-4138. This carries the existing possible identity with the Polwarth child Glasgow-1605 into a concrete local family model. The Polwarth index names the child’s father as William Glasgow, and Glasgow-2462 is already attached to that child with uncertainty. The three younger profile accounts are retained as possible stages of one life, not three proved brothers. Neither new father attachment is independent support for the other: both depend on the same child/adult identity and on the unproved identification of the named Polwarth father with the Inveresk man.

The Cavers man is the leading existing Scottish comparison for Glasgow-591 because the records establish a Covenanter and wreck survivor before the reported 1689 episode, while a probable member of his actual parish survivor group, James Young, appears among survivors said to have reached Ulster. Waddell’s 1886 account says all fifty survivors reached northern Ireland; his revised 1902 account says only some and omits both Glasgows from its named list. The omission does not exclude William, but the revision and late publication weaken the blanket migration claim. The 1684 Ormistoun record also prevents assuming uninterrupted Ulster residence from 1679. The later family history’s 1689 service and settlement remain tradition, not verified military service. No particular crossing, return journey, unit or Irish residence is invented. Its Cameron-to-Glasgow surname-origin story cannot explain a man already called Glasgow in 1679.

The weakest stage is the proposed father’s identity. Glasgow-2462 was born at Inveresk on 20 August 1639 and baptised the next day. He would have been only 18 at the 1658 Polwarth baptism and 16, nearly 17, at the associated Elizabeth baptism in August 1656. Young fatherhood is possible, but there is no marriage, residence or occupation connecting him with the named Polwarth father. An older, otherwise unidentified William is a substantial competing explanation. The named-child clause does not prove Glasgow-2462’s identity. The regional Polwarth/Gordon household of Glasgow-3107 is a stronger local kinship lead than Inveresk alone, but supplies no father clause for William; no exact brother, uncle or father relationship with James is selected. This inherited father remains a very low-confidence default and would fall away on both new adult accounts if the child/father identification fails. No mother is selected for either adult, and no wife or mother is transferred from the Inveresk ancestry.

This conditional Scottish parent model does not identify either of the two Hugh householders in the 1740 Tamlaght O’Crilly return. The inherited Glasgow-591 → Glasgow-551 → Glasgow-548 family-history sequence remains a separate question. The 1740 return and the 1772 parish declaration provide no evidence for the new Scottish father selections. No Tamlaght household identity or parent relationship becomes certain. See the complete comparison in Early Scottish records.

chapters.title: Two householders, not one family
body: The Protestant-householders return records two separate Hugh Glasgow entries, numbered 1195 and 1272 in the collector-order transcription. Both have townland recorded as ‘Not specified’.
The distinction is evidence against merging the entries. Age, occupation, wife, children and relationship are absent.

chapters.title: A geographic lead, not an address
body: Entry 1272 falls in a collector sequence with names independently found in the Inishrush leasehold community. A 1734 lease identifies several of those people at Inishrush, but no Glasgow is named.
That makes the sequence an Inishrush-linked lead; it does not make Hugh a stated resident or Margaret McCullough’s husband.

chapters.title: One later parish occurrence
body: A declaration dated at Innisrush names Hugh Glasgow among people described collectively as inhabitants of Tamlaght O’Crilly parish.
The notice gives no Hugh-specific townland, age or relatives. It could concern either older householder, the younger emigrant Hugh, or another namesake.

chapters.title: A family history stays qualified
body: A much later family history describes an older Hugh, Margaret McCullough and a younger Hugh. It is a research lead, not a record selecting either 1740 man.
The younger Hugh’s 1827 will establishes his later Pennsylvania household, but does not name his parents or an Irish connection to the recorded householders.

clusters.title: The two 1740 Hugh householders
clusters.summary: The return records two adult householders with the same name.
clusters.boundary: It does not identify either with a profile, townland or family.

clusters.title: The later Hugh traditions
clusters.summary: The 1772 name and later family account suggest questions worth testing.
clusters.boundary: Neither source assigns the parish occurrence or proves a traditional descent. The new very uncertain Scottish father model for the traditional William supplies no new identification of the parish Hugh.

links.label: The 1772 Hugh cannot be assigned to either 1740 household

proved: A Hugh present in the parish declaration of 1772.
supported: Entry 1272 is in an Inishrush-linked collector sequence.
hypothesis: One 1740 man was the older Hugh of the family tradition.
unresolved: Each householder's identity, relatives, townland and later life.
